posts.title: From $500 to $1 million in ten trading days: a Reddit options run, read off NVDA's chart
posts.summary: A Reddit account went from about $2,600 to $1,021,075 between 11 and 25 November 2026 by buying cheap, short-dated NVDA options with a fifth to a half of the account each time; four overnight gaps produced 81% of the profit shown, and the last position was worth $740,000 at 9:32 am and $95,000 by the close.

posts.title: Options for someone who trades stocks: a primer
posts.summary: An option is a rented, expiring, leveraged position in a stock; the huge gains in screenshots come from buying cheap options that expire soon, in size, just before a move larger than the market had priced in, and the same recipe loses the whole stake on most other days.

posts.title: Making room for luck: a reading of the Luck Field Manual, with the evidence checked
posts.summary: A popular 33-rule guide says luck can be engineered; its ideas reduce to three jobs (meet more chances, survive the bad ones, notice the good ones), the research behind them is strong for some rules and thin for others, and the advice only works where a failed attempt is cheap.

posts.title: Hedge funds, concentrated bets and short selling: a primer on big positions, public pressure and the cost of being early
posts.summary: A hedge fund is a private partnership that may borrow, sell short and put most of its money into a few positions, and the record shows that these freedoms produced a handful of famous results while the average fund, after fees, trailed both a plain index fund and a 60/40 portfolio over the last ten and twenty years.

posts.title: Bill Ackman: ten positions and capital that cannot leave
posts.summary: Ackman's audited record is about 16% a year since 2004 from roughly ten large positions and a few cheap hedges, but it includes four losing years in a row, and the listed fund has trailed the S&P 500 since its own launch in 2012.

posts.title: Michael Burry: the price of being early
posts.summary: Burry's one documented record (2000 to mid-2008, about 26% a year after fees, known from investor letters) came from reading documents nobody else read and from bets whose loss was capped at a premium; since 2008 no returns have been published, and his public market warnings since 2019 were followed by a higher index far more often than by a lower one.
